metadata.title: A machine learning analysis of school-level drivers of organisational innovativeness

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD TALIS 2018 principal data from 47 education systems (9,247 schools) and fits a single pooled model rather than building country-specific models. The authors state that the TALIS dataset includes sampling weights at the teacher and school levels to ensure national representativeness within each jurisdiction, but they do not report applying any TALIS weight variables in their ML workflow. Instead, they treat all observations meeting inclusion criteria as contributing equally to the pooled analysis. For data preparation, they exclude cases with missing values on the dependent variable (T3PORGIN), convert TALIS missing codes (−99) to NaN, impute missing predictor values using KNNImputer (k=5) after standardizing predictors, and then standardize predictors again for model training; they also use an 80/20 train/test split with 5-fold CV on the training set.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is the TALIS organisational innovativeness scale (T3PORGIN), constructed from four-point Likert items and treated as a direct scale score rather than an ILSA achievement PV outcome. Missing data handling is reported: the authors convert TALIS −99 codes to NaN and impute missing predictor values using KNN (k=5) while excluding cases with missing T3PORGIN from modelling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 school principal data for ISCED level 2 (lower secondary). The dependent variable is organisational innovativeness (T3PORGIN), derived from four principal questionnaire items (TC3G28A–D) on a four-point Likert scale. The analytic sample includes only principals with complete data on T3PORGIN; the authors excluded 455 observations with missing T3PORGIN. From the initial 303 school-level variables, they removed predictors with >12% missingness and then removed variables from highly correlated pairs (pairwise Pearson r>0.60), keeping the member with the lower missing-data rate; after these filters, 221 variables remained for analysis. Missing predictor values (coded as −99 in TALIS) were converted to NaN and imputed using KNNImputer (k=5) after standardizing predictors; the dependent variable was not imputed.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teachers can rely on each other

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Principal survey), ISCED Level 2, organisational innovativeness (T3PORGIN)
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best): RMSE=1.7350, MAE=1.3402, R²=0.2929. Other models: LightGBM RMSE=1.7421 MAE=1.3482 R²=0.2871; Linear Regression RMSE=1.7442 MAE=1.3658 R²=0.2853; SVR RMSE=1.7530 MAE=1.3441 R²=0.2781; Random Forest RMSE=1.7707 MAE=1.3691 R²=0.2635; Decision Tree RMSE=1.8297 MAE=1.3910 R²=0.2136.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 principal data (ISCED Level 2) to predict organisational innovativeness (T3PORGIN), the study leveraged school climate indicators (e.g., staff initiative encouragement, collaborative mutual support, shared responsibility, and cooperation with the local community) and time shortage with students to produce the best-performing model with XGBoost (RMSE=1.7350, MAE=1.3402, R²=0.2929). SHAP interpretation showed that supportive, participatory, and outward-looking school climates dominate the prediction, while time shortage with students reduces predicted innovativeness. This indicates that strengthening participatory school-climate routines and protecting implementation time may be more actionable for fostering school innovativeness than isolated structural changes, though the results are predictive associations rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD TALIS 2018 principal data from 47 education systems (ISCED Level 2) to predict organisational innovativeness (T3PORGIN), a scale derived from four principal Likert items. After excluding principals with missing T3PORGIN (final N=8,792) and imputing missing predictor values (−99 to NaN) via KNN (k=5) while standardizing predictors, the authors benchmarked six regression ML algorithms using an 80/20 train/test split and 5-fold CV on the training set. XGBoost achieved the best test performance (RMSE=1.7350, MAE=1.3402, R²=0.2929), outperforming LightGBM, Linear Regression, SVR, Random Forest, and a Decision Tree. SHAP was then used to rank influential TALIS items: school climate dominated (e.g., encouraging staff initiatives, mutual support, shared responsibility, community cooperation), principals’ job satisfaction was a strong secondary block, and time shortage with students showed a negative association. The authors caution that the approach is predictive (not causal), uses pooled-sample patterns, and relies on principals’ self-reports; they also do not report applying TALIS sampling weights in the ML pipeline.
